body:
See: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/104359

TLDR: Checking every vector that is passed to the physics engine for NaNs is a waste of CPU cycles. If limited to dev mode then I think it would be acceptable.

Yes, I believe using macros to limit NaN/Infinite detection on passed Vectors to _**DEV mode only**_ is a nice approach.

Firstly, it won't impact the performance of production builds.
Secondly, as demonstrated in the linked issue #104359, there are indeed developers (not only myself) who may inadvertently introduce NaN Vectors at unexpected locations, leading to bugs or performance degradation. Having DEV mode validate NaN Vectors similar to dangling pointer checks would significantly help developers catch and fix issues at the earliest stage.

(In my case, I spent tons of time tracking down the where of the xxxx NaN Vector in my project come from, only to discover it was caused by a missing safety check in an algorithm. If Dev mode had flagged the NaN at its place, that would have identified the problem days earlier when the code was first written.)

Especially, the appearance of such NaN Vectors is often accidental, stemming from flaws in algorithm design that only produce NaN results under extreme conditions. This makes such bugs extremely difficult to reproduce during actual development.
Since everyone typically implements safety checks, most edge cases are handled safely. Which means only the most extreme scenarios where _multiple coincidences align_ and a safety check was accidentally omitted in the design will trigger the error, and even then only very rarely. For such extremely rare and un-reproducible bugs, effective debugging is nearly impossible without immediate on-site error reporting (and manually set breakpoint interruption) in DEV mode.

I was lucky this time because I was only three days away from my last stable build, so I could simply iterate through and verify all changes made within those three days. But imagine -- if this weren't a solo indie project, but rather Godot evolving into a commercial team development engine like Unity with dozens of collaborators, and this issue was discovered only after several weeks -- that debugging campaign would be an absolute disaster.
